questions.q: Which of the following is the correct order of the four rungs?
options: Digitisation, digitalisation, digital enablement, digital transformation
Digital enablement, digitisation, digitalisation, digital transformation
Digitisation, digital enablement, digitalisation, digital transformation
Digitalisation, digitisation, digital enablement, digital transformation
questions.why: Each rung only stands on the one below it. You cannot make data flow before you have captured it, and you cannot equip people to act before the data flows.

questions.q: A company scans twenty years of paper registers into PDF files. This is:
questions.why: Converting a physical record to an electronic one, and nothing else. The work has not changed - the same steps happen on a different medium.

questions.q: A bank launches UPI payments so that transactions process themselves end to end. This is best described as:
questions.why: The system is now processing the transaction, not merely recording what a clerk did. That is the shift from holding data to moving and using it.

questions.q: Which of these is an OUTPUT rather than an outcome?
options: Cost leakage falls by two per cent
A decision that used to take a week now takes a day
Working capital cycle shortens by four days
Two hundred Power BI licences have been purchased
questions.why: A licence is a thing you now have - countable and photographable. The other three describe something that got measurably better, which makes them outcomes.

questions.q: The professor corrected a student who said the outcome of a new dashboard was 'access to data'. What was his correction?
options: The outcome is access to insight
The outcome is higher licence utilisation
The outcome is better data storage
questions.why: Data is still an output - a thing you hold. Insight is what lets somebody act. The distance between those two words is the distance between a project that pays for itself and one that does not.

questions.q: 'We do not have digital, we do digital' is a restatement of which distinction?
questions.why: The noun view lists what a company owns; the verb view lists what it does. Only the second is evidence that anything changed.

questions.q: Which of the following belongs in the VERB column of the digital estate?
questions.why: The first three are things that can be bought with a purchase order. Orchestrating and deciding are actions, and no purchase order buys them.

questions.q: Digital enablement is best defined as:
options: Converting physical records to electronic ones
Achieving a measurable improvement in margin
Equipping people and processes with tools, access and skills so the verbs can be performed
Buying the right tools at the right price
questions.why: Enablement is not owning the artefact - it is being able to act with it. Option C describes transformation, and option D describes digitisation.

questions.q: Which statement about digital enablement is FALSE according to the professor?
options: It is the destination rather than the journey
questions.why: That describes transformation, not enablement. Enablement is the work of getting there; transformation is where you end up. The other three are all things the professor said enablement is NOT.

questions.q: Data hygiene refers to:
options: How freely data moves between systems
Whether data is clean and trustworthy enough to use
questions.why: Hygiene is about condition. Movement between systems is liquidity, which is the next question.

questions.q: Data liquidity refers to:
options: How freely data moves between the places that need it
The accuracy of a single field
questions.why: A firm can have enormous volume and almost no liquidity, and it will feel exactly like a firm with no data at all.

questions.q: In the glacier analogy, the glass of clean drinking water represents:
questions.why: The glacier is the systems, the melt is the data flowing, and the glass is where value is finally consumed. Plenty of firms are proud of the glacier; few can hand you the glass.

questions.q: A change is called a transformation when it is:
options: Intended to be positive and lasting, judged on outcomes
questions.why: Scale, technology and board approval are all irrelevant. The word carries the intent inside it, and the judgement is made on outcomes rather than outputs.

questions.q: Which of the following is a PRIMARY activity in Porter's value chain?
questions.why: The five primary activities are inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and after-sales service. The other three options are support activities.

questions.q: In the value chain, information technology sits under:
questions.why: Note the distinction the professor drew: scientific technology - a better chemical composition for your product - sits under firm infrastructure. Information technology sits under technology development.

questions.q: Value, at its simplest, is:
questions.why: The size of the number is not the point; the size of the gap is. Everything else people call value is either a driver of that surplus or a consequence of it.

questions.q: The bottom line refers to:
options: Profit - what is left at the end
questions.why: It has nothing to do with hierarchy or with people at the top or bottom of an organisation. The top line is revenue.

questions.q: There are only two generic business positions. They are:
questions.why: Only two generic positions. A differentiator may compete on product or on customer closeness, but that is a split within one of the two, not a third position.

questions.q: A firm whose strategy is product differentiation spends its AI budget on cutting internal processing time. This is an example of:
questions.why: The cost lever is the right lever for a cost leader. For a differentiator, that money has been spent pulling the lever the strategy does not pay for.

questions.q: Efficiency converts into margin only when:
options: The technology is best in class
The freed capacity is absorbed by growth or genuinely removed
The saving is reported to the board
Utilisation of the tool is high
questions.why: Otherwise you have improved a ratio and changed no rupee. This is the fixed-cost objection raised in class, and it is the framework working rather than failing.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the doors for a firm's surplus?
options: Hold it indefinitely while telling shareholders to wait
questions.why: Reinvest, distribute, diversify are the three doors. Sitting on a surplus that earns nothing is what destroys value.

questions.q: Market capitalisation equals:
options: Shares outstanding multiplied by market price per share
questions.why: The market price reflects the whole expected future stream of profit, valued today - which is why both reinvesting well and paying dividends serve the shareholder.

questions.q: A smartphone maker begins manufacturing the semiconductors it consumes. This is:
questions.why: Backward means moving towards your suppliers, into your own inputs. Forward means moving towards the customer, into the next layer of your chain.

questions.q: The value SYSTEM is:
options: The support layer of the value chain
Your chain plus every connected chain - suppliers, channels, customers
questions.why: One firm's internal activities is the value chain. This distinction returns in Part 3 with the Viacom value system.

questions.q: A company deploys an ERP and internal reporting so its staff make better buying decisions. This is:
questions.why: The technology landed in the support layer and reached the value-creating work only indirectly, through people. That indirect route is the signature.

questions.q: A cab-hailing algorithm sets your price and allots your car with no human involved. This is the signature of:
questions.why: The algorithm is doing the value-creating work itself, with no human intermediary. That is the short circuit onto primary activities.

questions.q: An automated password-reset workflow inside the IT service desk is best classified as:
questions.why: It sits entirely inside one internal support flow. Impressive, but nothing in the value-creating chain moved.

questions.q: Business transformation is distinguished by the fact that:
options: It is the most expensive of the four
It touches only one process end to end
The dominant strategy moves and the business model changes
questions.why: Cost is not the test, and neither is the technology used. On the value chain map, the wedge is not merely widened - it is redrawn.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Cyber security and data privacy are the same control
Data privacy protects networks and devices from intrusion
Cyber security protects the individual behind the data
Data security protects the data itself, wherever it sits or moves
questions.why: Cyber security protects the systems; data privacy protects the individual behind the data. All three are handled by different controls.

questions.q: Why does pursuing DT change a firm's risk profile more than pursuing ITOT?
options: Because the attack surface moves to where value is actually created
Because ITOT has no security implications
Because DT requires cloud by definition
questions.why: ITOT puts technology behind your own staff. DT puts it directly in front of customers, so the exposure sits on the value-creating activity itself.

questions.q: The four building blocks in the anchoring reading are:
options: Leadership, collaboration, data empowerment, value realisation
questions.why: These four come from the anchoring reading. Scope, ways, means and ends is the separate strategic framework from

questions.q: Which building block did the professor add to the four in the reading?
questions.why: The reading has nothing about people's willingness to accept what the machine says, which is exactly the gap the card-company caselet exposes.

questions.q: A collaboration problem between departments is very often, in disguise:
questions.why: Whether departments share data is a culture question, and culture is set, raised or flattened by leadership. Diagnose them together or you fix the wrong one.

questions.q: In the logistics caselet, which TWO boxes of the IS Success Model were broken?
questions.why: Data arrived fragmented from several systems and was never believed; re-pulls took two days to two and a half months. System quality was present but not acute.

questions.q: Service quality, in the IS Success Model, is about:
options: Whether the vendor contract is well written
How responsive the internal team is when somebody queries a number
questions.why: The reconciliation and re-pull your data team performs is a service being delivered to an internal customer. Two days for a two-hour decision is a service failure, not a data failure.

questions.q: The reporting interface takes two minutes to launch on a Monday morning. This is a failure of:
questions.why: This is the artefact itself - does it load, respond and stay up. It destroys credibility just as effectively as a wrong number.

questions.q: The DeLone and McLean model added service quality as a separate dimension in:
questions.why: The original model is from 1992. Service quality was added as a separate dimension in the widely used 2003 revision.

questions.q: In the card-company caselet, which box was broken?
questions.why: Everything to the left was fine and usage was high. What failed was trust - they used it and then overrode it.

questions.q: Two thirds of underwriting decisions being overridden with no reason recorded is evidence that:
options: The users do not trust the output enough to act on it
questions.why: The model was accurate and the system was working. An override with no reason recorded is a satisfaction failure, which is why the fix was behavioural rather than technical.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Adoption is attitudinal; usage is behavioural
Adoption and usage are the same thing measured differently
Adoption is behavioural; usage is attitudinal
questions.why: Adoption comes first and lives in the head. Usage comes later and shows up in the logs. Getting this backwards is the most common error in this part.

questions.q: The Technology Acceptance Model rests on which two beliefs?
options: Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use
questions.why: Two beliefs, and only two, in the classical model. Training exists to move the second one.

questions.q: Everything to the left of adoption is described as 'perceived' because:
options: Nobody has used the thing yet, so these are beliefs not evidence
questions.why: We are still in the thinking phase rather than the doing phase, which is exactly why the dashed line on the diagram sits where it does.

questions.q: 'Continued intention to use' is the workplace equivalent of which marketing idea?
questions.why: Continued intention to use is the same idea, except that here your employees are the customers.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a usage metric?
questions.why: The other three measure the tool. Override rate measures whether the tool changed a decision, which is the only one on the road to margin.

questions.q: The single intervention that fixed the card-company problem was:
options: A new model with higher accuracy
Requiring a written justification for every override
questions.why: No new model, no new platform, no retraining. One change-management intervention.

questions.q: Why does requiring a justification work?
options: It makes reasoning visible, removes the effortlessness of overriding, and creates measurable data
It shifts accountability to the model
It reduces the number of decisions taken
questions.why: Three effects at once. Note that it does not remove the override - the professor was explicit that nothing was being forced down anybody's throat.

questions.q: An employee refuses to help improve an automation tool that could replace their role. This is best described as:
questions.why: No amount of training fixes it. What fixes it is leadership giving credible comfort that this is an enabler rather than a replacement, and then behaving consistently.

questions.q: The five readiness buckets are leadership, organisational, data, workforce and:
questions.why: It measures the head start that already exists - dashboards, data products, a reporting culture.

questions.q: On the readiness chart, an axis closer to the centre means:
questions.why: Further from the centre means more ready. The innermost axes are where the constraint sits, and therefore where the money should go.

questions.q: If data readiness is the innermost axis and decision intelligence the outermost, where should the money go?
questions.why: The first three all target axes that are already strong. Spending on a strength that is not the constraint buys almost nothing, because the inner axis still blocks the value.

questions.q: Workforce readiness scoring higher than organisational readiness suggests:
options: People are capable but the collective culture stalls the workflow
questions.why: Individually skilled, collectively stuck. That is cultural resistance, and it needs change management, not another training programme.

questions.q: The professor distinguished mistrust from distrust. Mistrust is:
options: A judgement you have formed about something
A refusal to use a system
questions.why: Distrust is a judgement you have formed about something. Mistrust is what bad data leaves you with - you simply cannot settle whether the number is right.

questions.q: For a quantitative survey, the Hair and Black rule of thumb is roughly:
options: Thirty per cent of the population
questions.why: Per individual question, not per bucket. With thirty-odd questions, forty-nine responses is thin but workable for a demonstration.

questions.q: In a qualitative study, you stop interviewing when:
options: The same pain points start repeating - saturation
Half the organisation has been covered
questions.why: In the professor's experience that shows up after seven or eight interviews, which is why five well-chosen respondents can be enough.

questions.q: Survey participation rates depend most on:
options: Who asks and how they ask
questions.why: A chief executive asking lands differently from a technology chief asking, and three live sessions land differently from one email. Same request, very different response rates.

questions.q: The story of moving the data chief's reporting line to the chief executive shows that:
options: Structure has no effect on outcomes
Data teams should report to technology
Every organisation design fixes something and breaks something else
questions.why: Moving the reporting line solved the influence problem and created a new one, where the data team stopped listening to the business. There is no correct chart.

questions.q: In the information systems triangle, a decision SUPPORT system is one where:
options: A human reads the output and decides
The system decides and acts alone
questions.why: If the output triggers an action with nobody in between, you are in decision automation - a different world with a different risk profile.

questions.q: How is decision automation properly earned?
options: By keeping a human in the loop for years, tracking disagreement, and removing the human only when error is negligible
By buying a more accurate model
questions.why: Redeploying that person afterwards is what the professor calls capability building.

questions.q: Which of the three data monetisation routes disappears inside a company that does not sell data externally?
questions.why: Inside a company that does not sell data externally, the third leg disappears and you are left with the first two - which map onto cost leadership and differentiation.

questions.q: In the published framework, big data analytics ranks last of eight themes because:
options: It was added late to the paper
It behaves like a hygiene factor - presence earns nothing, absence stops everything
questions.why: Herzberg's idea, applied to technology. It is the vehicle, not the destination, which is the argument the whole module opened with.

questions.q: Incremental value creation describes:
options: Growing an already positive surplus year on year
Cutting the workforce to protect margin
Recovering value that has been lost
questions.why: The ordinary ambition of a healthy firm - reinforce technology, train people, tighten the line, and the triangle gets bigger.

questions.q: Value re-creation is the correct response when:
options: The company is already the cost leader
The company has spotted a new market
The company's value is shrinking and must be recovered
questions.why: A different brief from growth. Fund a growth programme for a company that needs a repair programme and you get General Electric.

questions.q: Viacom's top line fell roughly ten per cent while profit fell roughly forty per cent. The correct reading is:
options: Costs were fixed and could not be cut
Market share is going AND the spend to hold customers is not converting
The auditors changed the accounting policy
questions.why: You have to read both lines together. A bottom line falling four times faster than the top line means the retention effort has become pure operating cost.

questions.q: Migrating from an in-house ERP to SAP is best classified as:
questions.why: Same transactions, same approvals, same invoices, same audit trails. The system sits in the support activities. Useful and expensive, but the business is not somewhere new.

questions.q: An outward-facing need typically leads to which value discipline and which line?
questions.why: Outward-facing needs are opportunistic. You are chasing a new market or a new product, so you differentiate and you aim at revenue.

questions.q: An inward-facing need is characterised by:
options: A shortcoming in the existing set-up
questions.why: Top line going, margins squeezed, customers leaving. You still transform, but towards plugging leakages and efficiency - cost leadership, aimed at the bottom line.

questions.q: Adding sensors so a car achieves a five-star safety rating at the same price is an example of:
questions.why: The uniqueness sits in the product itself, and everything else stays as it is.

questions.q: Free lifetime roadside assistance and a buyback agreement on an unchanged car is an example of:
questions.why: Same car, same production line. What changed is the relationship around the product, not the metal.

questions.q: The shift from corner shops to ten-minute delivery for the same packet of biscuits is:
questions.why: The biscuits have not changed. No travel, no waiting, pre-delivery and loyalty are all customer-centric interventions layered on an unchanged product.

questions.q: Why does it matter WHO is driving a transformation?
options: Because regulators require a named owner
Because it changes the technology stack
Because a leader-championed programme is steered and executed very differently from a bottom-up one
questions.why: When the need was sensed at the top, leadership is committed from the start. When it arrives as a complaint after bad results, the leader may never fully commit.

questions.q: In the Viacom data journey, the metering devices in homes solved which problem and created which?
options: Solved generalisability, but the unit of measurement was still the household
Solved data quality, created a privacy breach
questions.why: Grandparents, parents and children all watched the same set, so family-level viewing stayed scattered and varied. Still generalised, just at a finer grain.

questions.q: The unit of measurement finally became one person when:
questions.why: And that is exactly when the appetite for data exploded and decision-making got paralysed - they were capturing far more than they could use.

questions.q: 'T minus K' expresses the idea that:
options: Data must be refreshed every K minutes
Every dashboard shows data that has already happened, K being the delay
Latency can be reduced to zero with sensors
questions.why: K can be squeezed but never made zero, and never negative. Which is why moving from measures of what happened to predictions of what will happen is the hinge of the Viacom case.

questions.q: Value co-creation means:
options: Internal departments collaborating on a project
Selling data to a third party
Separate firms, each with their own value chain, all ending up better off
questions.why: Internal departments collaborating is collaboration, not co-creation. A value chain is drawn from the point of view of a single firm.

questions.q: In the Viacom value system, what do advertising agencies receive?
options: Pricing and slot predictions before signing
Access to the raw customer database
questions.why: Viacom's ability to predict was more mature than theirs, so they trusted its judgement over their own - and both sides negotiated faster as a result.

questions.q: Co-opetition is best described as:
options: Rivals cooperating in a defined space where all gain, while competing elsewhere
questions.why: Option A is lobbying - collective pressure applied to a third party. Co-opetition creates value none of the participants could create alone.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five ingredients (means)?
questions.why: The five are organisational capabilities, leadership, workforce, data governance and analytics. Market share is an outcome, not an ingredient.

questions.q: In the 2024 paper, leadership originally sat:
questions.why: It was pulled out as a separate ingredient afterwards, on the strength of practitioner work rather than the paper. Know which version you are quoting.

questions.q: Which three things sit under organisational capabilities?
options: Culture, structure and design, decision making
questions.why: Processes and innovation were both folded back into culture when the class offered them separately.

questions.q: An organisation with a long history of subjective, expert-based decisions is likely to:
options: Resist model-driven decision autonomy at first
questions.why: It is the opposite habit. Objective decision cultures accept model outputs naturally; discretionary ones fight it, at least for the first months or years.

questions.q: The professor's conclusion on leadership and culture is that the relationship is:
options: Two-way - each constrains and scales the other
questions.why: The Bengali instruction shows culture doing the work rather than authority. The email story shows a sixty-year-old culture shaping how every leader behaves.

questions.q: In the Oracle-to-SAP migration example, the root cause of the inertia was:
options: The new system was technically inferior
Perceived usefulness at the individual level was close to zero
questions.why: Same transactions, same approvals, same audit trails. The organisation gained scale; the user gained nothing and lost their comfort.

questions.q: Which pairing of problem and fix is correct?
options: Ability gap - fixed with change management
Ability gap - fixed with training and exposure
Attitude gap - fixed with better software
questions.why: Attitude gaps need change management, communication and something genuinely in it for the user. Spending training money on an attitude problem is the classic and expensive mix-up.

questions.q: The big bang data strategy failed at the Asia-Pacific bank mainly because:
options: It was never aligned to a business use case before starting
questions.why: Three years later only occasional analysts wanting historical data could use it, and real-time needs were never in scope.

questions.q: In the kitchen analogy, the correct approach is:
options: Chop onions fresh for every order
Make one base gravy in the morning and build dishes from it
Cook the whole menu in advance
questions.why: One base, many users, improved over time, components reused. That base gravy is the data product idea in one image.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of the grassroots architecture?
options: Revenue defined three different ways by three departments
questions.why: Lack of standardisation is a grassroots problem. Slow builds and heavy capital cost belong to the monolith, and adoption is one of grassroots' genuine strengths.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of the monolithic architecture?
questions.why: Control buys symmetry and installs guardrails. Pulling data off a server needs skills and access a business user usually does not have.

questions.q: In the hybrid design, where exactly is the cut made?
options: After the lakehouse, inserting a data product layer
questions.why: Keep the monolith up to that point, because that is where its uniformity comes from. Then restore grassroots freedom on the other side.

questions.q: Data products are typically shipped as CSV rather than XLSX because CSV:
options: Is lightweight, machine readable and has no row ceiling
questions.why: If your user base grows and the format caps out at around a million rows, your product is obsolete. CSV also avoids the encoding complications of a spreadsheet format.

questions.q: Which statement about data governance is correct?
options: Data governance is a subset of cyber security
Data governance and data quality are the same thing
questions.why: Quality is one building block inside it, alongside ownership, rights, stewardship, classification, access and accountability.

questions.q: A firm has a mature reporting estate, twelve crore already spent, high dashboard usage - and working capital, cost leakage and the top line have all been flat for eight quarters. What is the correct first move?
options: Walk back up the IS Success chain and find which box is broken
Escalate to the board for more investment
Replace the reporting tool with a better one
questions.why: Everything to the left may look fine while satisfaction or service quality is quietly failing. Buying a new tool fixes one box out of six.

questions.q: Which pairing of monetisation route and value discipline is correct?
questions.why: Plugging leakage and deciding faster serves the cost leader. Wrapping data around what you already sell serves the differentiator.

questions.q: A company's need is inward facing - shrinking margins and eroding customers - but its transformation programme is built around launching a premium connected product. What is the problem?
options: The need and the chosen value discipline do not match
There is nothing wrong; both branches are always valid
questions.why: Inward-facing needs point to cost leadership and the bottom line. Building a premium offering pulls the lever the situation does not pay for.

questions.q: Put these in the order a company must actually achieve them:
questions.why: You cannot make data flow before you have captured it, and you cannot package a clean, reusable mart before the data flows.

questions.q: Rolling out training on a new assistant tool across the whole workforce is best described as:
questions.why: Buying the licences would be procurement, a noun. Equipping people so the verb can actually be performed is enablement.

questions.q: A readiness chart shows leadership at 4.2 and data readiness at 3.2. The company buys a new reporting tool. What should you predict?
options: Improvement in year two once training completes
Little or no improvement, because the constraint was never the tool
Improvement only in the finance function
A significant improvement, since leadership is behind it
questions.why: Money into an existing strength buys almost nothing. The innermost axis still blocks the value from coming out.

questions.q: Which sequence of frameworks answers the two questions 'will they use it?' and 'did using it change anything?'
options: The IS Success Model, then the acceptance model
The acceptance model, then the IS Success Model
questions.why: Acceptance tells you whether they will adopt. The IS Success Model tells you whether adoption produced any net benefit.

questions.q: In which of the four transformations is the value wedge redrawn rather than merely widened?
questions.why: Business transformation is where the dominant strategy moves and the model itself changes. The others widen the wedge without redrawing it.

questions.q: A vehicle manufacturer gives its five hundred suppliers visibility of forward demand, and charges for it. This is:
questions.why: The data has become the offering. Suppliers pay because it frees working capital that was locked in inventory.

questions.q: In the Viacom value system, how many independent value chains are involved?
options: Five - Viacom plus advertisers, content creators, regulators and competitors
Five, but only Viacom's value rises
questions.why: And the whole point is that every one of the five ends up better off - which is what separates co-creation from collaboration.

questions.q: You install more sensors and increase refresh frequency on a dashboard. What happens to T minus K?
options: K is unaffected by refresh rate
K gets smaller but never reaches zero
questions.why: A dashboard is always retrospective. Squeezing the delay is worth doing, but if you want to see forward you have to move from measures to predictions.

questions.q: In the hybrid architecture the professor recommends, what typically sits on premise and what on cloud?
options: The lakehouse on premise, the data products on cloud
The data products on premise, the lakehouse on cloud
questions.why: Users hold credentials and fetch the product they need into a dashboard or a hosted analysis environment.

questions.q: A team shows high login frequency and a high override rate. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: Use is fine; satisfaction has failed
questions.why: They open it and they mean to - that is use. They do not trust it enough to act on it - that is satisfaction.

questions.q: Which element of the framework behaves like a hygiene factor?
questions.why: Having it earns you nothing; not having it stops everything. It is the vehicle, not the destination.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT sit under organisational capabilities?
questions.why: Workforce is its own ingredient in the list of five, precisely because ability and attitude behave differently from culture and structure.

questions.q: The professor's own definition of data culture is:
options: Every decision must be justified with numbers
The chief data officer reports to the chief executive
Everybody has access to a dashboard
Data is treated as another product line, nurtured like any other product
questions.why: He is deliberate about not calling it data culture. Once data is a product line, no leader gets to look at it in their own private fragmented way.

questions.q: Why does the grassroots architecture usually show better adoption than the monolith?
options: It has a single source of truth
Whoever built the pipeline built it for that specific business owner
questions.why: Few hops, instant feedback loop, and the same person who wrote the rules fixes it when it breaks.

questions.q: Which statement correctly pairs each failure with its cause?
options: Big bang failed on reusability; grassroots failed on alignment to use cases
Big bang failed on alignment to use cases; grassroots failed on reusability
questions.why: The bank cleaned and dumped everything without asking what anybody needed. The grassroots teams built one-off pipelines nobody else could use.

questions.q: Three departments walk into the chief executive's room with three different revenue figures and spend fifteen minutes reconciling them. The root cause is:
options: Lack of standardisation and no single source of truth
questions.why: One team counts units, one counts rupees, one counts tonnes. This is the classic grassroots cost.

questions.q: 'Who may share this data without first removing the names from it?' is a question belonging to:
questions.why: Governance covers ownership, definitions, quality protocols, access, sharing and anonymisation. Security protects; governance decides.

questions.q: A bank moves loan approval from fifteen days of paperwork to a two-day automated workflow. This is:
questions.why: One horizontal process rebuilt end to end, narrow by design. The business model has not moved.

questions.q: The same bank then launches a mobile-first proposition - accounts opened in minutes, instant algorithmic lending, branches turned advisory. This is:
questions.why: The dominant strategy has moved and the revenue model is new. The wedge is redrawn, not widened.

questions.q: Which sequence is correct?
options: Intention, adoption, use, satisfaction, continued intention
questions.why: Everything before adoption is belief. Everything after it is observable. Continued intention is the repeat-purchase equivalent.

questions.q: Which sequence describes the IS Success Model correctly?
options: Use, then the three qualities, then satisfaction
Satisfaction, then net benefits, then the three qualities
The three qualities, then use and satisfaction, then net benefits
Net benefits, then the three qualities, then use
questions.why: Technology, then behaviour, then strategic outcome. That order is what makes it a diagnostic path rather than a scorecard.

questions.q: Data readiness is the weakest axis on a readiness chart. A vendor proposes a new self-service analytics platform. The best response is:
options: Decline for now and unify the data first, because the platform will surface the same distrusted numbers faster
Buy it but delay the rollout by a year
Buy it - self-service will solve the queue
Buy it only for the finance team
questions.why: A faster route to a number nobody believes does not produce a decision. Fix the innermost axis first.

questions.q: An AI deployment frees two hours of work per person per day, but the cost base is fixed and nobody is redeployed. The honest claim to make is:
options: A ratio has improved but no rupee has changed
Cost has fallen by the value of two hours per person
questions.why: Efficiency converts into margin only when the freed capacity is absorbed by growth or genuinely removed. This is the fixed-cost objection from class.

questions.q: In the Balanced Scorecard, training, knowledge and capability building sit under which perspective?
questions.why: And learning and growth feeds internal process, which feeds customer, which feeds financial. That chain is how a soft benefit reaches a hard number.

questions.q: RATER stands for:
questions.why: The five criteria of SERVQUAL, which is where the service quality dimension of the IS Success Model comes from.

questions.q: Garvin's eight dimensions of quality apply primarily to:
questions.why: Performance, features, reliability, conformance, durability, serviceability, aesthetics and perceived quality. SERVQUAL is the services parallel.

questions.q: Which stakeholder in the Viacom value system receives an early read on what is likely to clear screening?
questions.why: Fewer surprises for them, and Viacom avoids signing contracts that will not pass.

questions.q: Two rival payment providers pool transaction data under agreed rules and each earns from the shared analysis. Two other rivals jointly petition a regulator not to enforce a rule. These are, respectively:
questions.why: Co-opetition creates value none of them could create alone. Lobbying applies collective pressure to a third party.

questions.q: A company runs three hundred systems and every department builds its own pipeline. Which cost appears first and keeps recurring?
options: Capital expenditure on the data platform
The cost of hiring a chief data officer
Licensing cost for the reporting tool
Operating cost from doing the same cleaning several times over
questions.why: You burn the same computing resource repeatedly for no new information. That is a recurring running cost, not a one-off.

questions.q: The cleanest test of whether something is genuinely a data product is:
options: Is it stored in the cloud?
Pull the data out - does the business still run?
Does more than one department use it?
questions.why: Take data out of a cab-hailing app and no cab gets booked and no price gets set. At that point data is core, not support.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason data products are shipped as CSV rather than as a spreadsheet file?
options: It has no practical row ceiling
It is supported natively by reporting tools
It is lightweight and machine readable
questions.why: Formulas and formatting are exactly what you do not want in a data product - it is a clean, reusable dataset, not a working document.

questions.q: The fifth building block - workforce - was added to the reading's four because of which case?
options: The card company where everything worked and value still did not appear
The logistics company with the distrusted dashboard
questions.why: Data, service and system quality were all fine there. The only thing broken was people's willingness to act on the output.

questions.q: What does the T minus K idea imply about a company that wants to become predictive?
options: It must move from measures of what happened to forecasts of what will happen
It should centralise its data team
It should reduce the number of dashboards
questions.why: Squeezing the delay makes a backward-looking view fresher. It never makes it forward-looking. That extension is the hinge of the Viacom case.

questions.q: A transformation is proposed. Which pair of questions should you ask first?
options: Which vendor, and at what price?
What is the need, and who is driving it?
What is the cloud strategy, and who owns it?
How many licences, and for whom?
questions.why: The need tells you which value discipline you are pulling on. Who is driving it tells you more about the odds than the technology stack ever will.

questions.q: Which statement about digitisation in the Viacom story is correct?
options: It happened only after streaming arrived
Once capture became automatic, the money moved from collection into building data pipelines
questions.why: Same budget line, completely different purpose - and a good illustration that digitisation is an antecedent, not a substitute.

questions.q: Change management for digital transformation is specifically about:
options: Retraining the workforce on a new tool
Realigning how data teams interact with technology teams, business users and processes, in phases
questions.why: Look back at the failures in this document and count how many were technical. Almost none were.

questions.q: Which single sentence best captures the module?
options: Automate everything a human currently decides
Buy the best technology you can afford
It is not about what we have; it is about what we do
questions.why: Every distinction in this document - output against outcome, artefact against enablement, adoption against usage - is that one sentence in a different costume.
